item.text: {"text":"[NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) uses causal dilated convolutions and residual blocks to capture long-range dependencies. A direct mechanism for suppressing shortcut information comes from [Highway Networks](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2015/file/215a71a12769b056c3c32e7299f1c5ed-Paper.pdf): independently gate transformed and carried features, y=T(x)⊙H(x)+C(x)⊙x. Applied within NextItNet, this would permit attenuation of the shortcut as well as convolution outputs; gating only the update leaves an unrestricted identity path. This is an architectural hypothesis, not an established NextItNet forgetting result. Moreover, suppressing mixed hidden features does not guarantee selective removal of older evidence: temporal selection must also govern which historical positions enter convolution paths.\n\nRecent adjacent evidence supports testing relevance and session structure, without establishing that older interactions are inherently harmful. [DyS4Rec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608025000139) targets irrelevant historical interactions through adaptive skipping. [Session-aware recommendation research (2025)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/10902109) introduces session tokens, segment embeddings and temporal attention, evaluated in recurrent and attention architectures. Neither directly validates forgetting throughout NextItNet. A suitable single-network experiment would compare the corrected baseline, a retrained bounded-history control, fixed temporal decay, and learned causal gates using timestamp gaps or session boundaries. Apply temporal restrictions consistently across convolution paths; gate residual carries where representations already contain history. Evaluate all variants using the same macro validation HR@10. Sparse replacement probes alone cannot establish stale-history harm; gains from truncation or decay would provide stronger task-specific evidence."}
